content: 1. Any requirements that fail to meet the established standards will be classified as defective. 2. The acceptance number represents the maximum allowable number of defective samples for a lot to be deemed acceptable. 3. The number of containers or samples to be drawn from a lot, as well as the acceptance number, is specified in the provided table. 4. For lots containing 300 or fewer containers, 13 samples must be tested, with an acceptance number of 0. For lots with 301 to 1200 containers, 21 samples must be tested, with an acceptance number of 1. For lots with 1201 to 2000 containers, 29 samples must be tested, with an acceptance number of 2. For lots with 2001 to 7000 containers, 48 samples must be tested, with an acceptance number of 3. For lots with 7001 to 15000 containers, 84 samples must be tested, with an acceptance number of 5. For lots with 15001 to 24000 containers, 126 samples must be tested, with an acceptance number of 7. For lots with 24001 to 41000 containers, 123 samples must be tested, with an acceptance number of 10. For lots exceeding 41000 containers, 346 samples must be tested, with an acceptance number of 13. 5. Each container or sample to be tested must be randomly selected from a different master carton. Random number tables should be used to ensure randomness. If such tables are unavailable, a systematic method may be employed, where every rth carton is selected, with r being the integral part of N/n (N = total number of master cartons in the lot, n = number of master cartons to be selected). 6. The weight and shape of the product should be described in a note to distinguish it from others. 7. Analytical methods must comply with CIPAC, AOAC, or equivalent standards. If unpublished methods are used, full details and appropriate validation data must be submitted to FAO/WHO by the proposer. 8. Samples must be sufficiently large to conduct all required tests and must be representative of the product. A sufficient quantity of samples must be randomly selected, and in some cases, the total amount of the product must be used. 9. If the product has different types (e.g., coating and incorporation), each type should be sampled and tested separately. 10. Use sharp scissors or equivalent tools to minimize damage to the product and avoid bias in test results. Place a small portion in a labeled, new, clean screw-glass bottle before analysis. 11. Samples should be kept cool, avoiding heat sources (including sunlight) or freezing, and analyzed/tested with minimal delay. 12. For chemical analysis, the analytical method and the number and size of test portions analyzed should be designed to provide applicable results. 13. Test portion and replication requirements for physical test methods should be defined in the referenced methods or notes. 14. Methods for determining retention/release rates and the criteria for product retention/release rates may be product-specific. 15. This clause or sub-clause is required only if appropriate to the specified product. 16. The isomer ratio is specified only when the active ingredient is defined as a particular isomer ratio. 17. A synergist is specified only when required. 18. An impurity is specified only when it is relevant, as defined in the glossary of terms (Appendix C). 19. The method of analysis must be peer-validated at a minimum. If unpublished, full details of the method and peer-validation data must be provided. 20. Whether a final product sinks or floats on water depends on the type of polymer used. This property is closely related to the application method and must be specified. 21. To test whether the product sinks or floats, drop one piece of the product into a sufficiently large beaker containing CIPAC standard water D. Stir thoroughly with a glass rod to ensure complete wetting and remove air bubbles. After one minute, state the test result as either sinking or floating. 22. Unless otherwise specified, alternative storage conditions include six weeks at 45 ± 2°C, eight weeks at 40 ± 2°C, twelve weeks at 35 ± 2°C, or eighteen weeks at 30 ± 2°C. The whole product must be stored under these conditions. 23. Samples of the product taken before and after the storage stability test should be analyzed concurrently to reduce analytical error. 24. When the entire product is used to analyze the active ingredient/synergist, the tolerance of the product should be examined and described. 25. This sub-clause is required only if the relevant impurity concentration is capable of increasing during storage. 26. A long-lasting treated storage bag is defined as a woven polymer fiber bag with a pesticide active ingredient incorporated into the fiber or coated on its surface. 27. The storage bag is intended for post-harvest storage of commodities such as cereal grains, pulses, and seeds, providing pest control over a specified time period (at least two years, over multiple seasons). 28. The pesticide is released to the surface of the material in a sustained manner, ensuring continuous protection against pest infestation. 29. To evaluate the migration of the active ingredient, the proposed methodology is adapted from the CIPAC method MT 195 (Wash resistance index of long-lasting nets). 30. If the fiber material is a polyolefin (e.g., HDPE, PP), an anti-slip weave in the weaving pattern is recommended to increase frictional force between stacked bags and reduce the hazard of falling bags. 31. The presence of an anti-slip weave may be checked by visual inspection, counting ends versus picks, and comparison with known anti-slip weaving patterns. This feature should be noted on the storage bag label. 32. The polymer material used to produce the yarn must be virgin (non-recycled) polymer and comply with international regulations concerning food contact materials. 33. Migration of polyolefins must be tested as per US FDA 21 CFR Part 177-1520 or EU Directive 10/2011 for food contact substances. 34. Migration of heavy metals must be tested as per BS EN 1186:2002 or TIS-656-2529 (1986) or other suitable ASTM methods, ensuring the sum concentration levels of lead, cadmium, mercury, and hexavalent chromium do not exceed 100 ppm. 35. Residues of pesticides incorporated or coated in the bag on the stored commodity should comply with the Codex Alimentarius Maximum Residue Levels (MRLs) for the pesticide and commodity combinations. 36. Manufacturers should control and minimize within-product heterogeneity of the active ingredient and provide a sub-sampling scheme to represent the active ingredient of the product unit. 37. Physical properties and testing of long-lasting treated storage bags in this guideline are harmonized with ISO standard 23560:2015. 38. If a claim for UV stability is made, the clause for UV stability must be included. 39. Methods for identification and determination of the active ingredient content must comply with CIPAC, AOAC, or equivalent standards. 40. Sampling schemes should consider within-product variation. Homogenization of samples before and after storage and keeping the sample in a capped bottle are recommended. 41. Samples must be sufficiently large to conduct all required tests and be representative of the fabric. 42. Use sharp scissors or equivalent tools to minimize damage to the fibers and fabric, avoiding bias in test results. 43. Samples should be kept cool, avoiding heat sources or freezing, and analyzed/tested with minimal delay. 44. Methods for determining isomer ratios must be peer-validated. 45. The CIPAC method MT 195 for determining the wash resistance index of LN was adopted as a full CIPAC method in 2013 but is not yet published in a Handbook. 46. Methods for determining relevant impurities must be peer-validated at a minimum. 47. The manufacturer must demonstrate that the sub-sampling design provides homogenized analytical portions for before and after storage stability tests. 48. For accelerated storage testing, the entire bag is stored at 54 ± 2°C for two weeks, and appropriate samples are taken after storage from the bag. 49. Representative portions for testing should be taken as described in each test method. 50. Long-lasting pesticide-treated storage bags are expected to retain their biological activity and tensile strength during their lifespan and through exposure to UV over a specified number of hours. 51. Flammability of the product is not part of the specification but should be measured by the manufacturer according to 16 CFR Part 1610, with the result presented on the package. 52. The sampling scheme should consider within-product variation, and homogenization of samples before and after storage is recommended.
